theme: A time for everything; oppression and friendship
readingInstruction: Read Ecclesiastes 3:1-4:16. This includes the famous poem about time and the Preacher’s reflections on oppression, envy, and companionship. Read the poem slowly.
settingTheScene: The Preacher continues his reflection. Having seen that effort alone cannot satisfy, he now considers the structure of time itself. Chapter 3 is among the most quoted passages in the Bible, and chapter 4 returns to the harsh realities of oppression and loneliness, and offers a consolation in the value of friendship.
observation: “For everything there is a season, and a time for every matter under heaven” (3:1).
“A time to be born, and a time to die… a time to weep, and a time to laugh… a time to mourn, and a time to dance” (3:2-4).
“He has made everything beautiful in its time” (3:11).
“Also, he has put eternity into man’s heart, yet so that he cannot find out what God has done from the beginning to the end” (3:11).
“I perceived that there is nothing better for them than to be joyful and to do good as long as they live” (3:12).
“I perceived that whatever God does endures forever” (3:14).
“And I saw all the oppressions that are done under the sun. And behold, the tears of the oppressed, and they had no one to comfort them” (4:1).
“Two are better than one, because they have a good reward for their toil” (4:9).
interpretation:
The poem of times is a catalog of fourteen pairs of opposite experiences: birth and death, planting and uprooting, weeping and laughing, embracing and refraining. It affirms that life has seasons, and that God governs them. It is not saying that all things are good, but that there is a time for everything, including grief. We are not meant to be always joyful or always sorrowful. Wisdom discerns the time.

The central statement is verse 11. God has made everything beautiful in its time. And he has put “eternity into man’s heart.” We have a sense of something beyond the present. We long for the permanent in a world of passing things. But we cannot see the whole picture. We live in the middle of the story and cannot grasp its end. This is why we are restless. The longing for eternity is a pointer to God. We are made for more than this world offers.

The Preacher’s response is not despair but a call to receive life as a gift: be joyful, do good, eat and drink, and see it as the gift of God. And he reminds us of a comforting truth: “Whatever God does endures forever.” Human works fade, but God’s work stands. “God has done it, so that people fear before him.”

Chapter 4 gives an honest view of injustice. The oppressed weep, and “they had no one to comfort them.” The Preacher is moved by it, and he does not offer a quick answer. He sees envy driving much of human labor and sees the loneliness of those who work without end.

The balance comes in the section on companionship. “Two are better than one.” If one falls, the other lifts him. Two keep warm. And the line, “A threefold cord is not quickly broken,” has become a proverb for marriage and friendship. In a world of vapor, relationships are among the few things that give strength.
connection: Galatians 4:4 says, “When the fullness of time had come, God sent forth his Son.” The time of Christ’s coming was God’s chosen time. Jesus wept (John 11:35) and danced no less with joy (Luke 15:25-32), and entered all the seasons of human experience. Romans 8:18-25 describes our groaning as we wait. Jesus sent his disciples out two by two (Luke 10:1). Hebrews 10:24-25 urges believers not to neglect meeting together.
application:
Ask what season you are in. What is God asking of you in it?

Notice the “eternity” longing in your heart, and let it point you to God.

Think of a friend you can strengthen or lean on this week.
prayerPrompts: Ask God to help you discern the season you are in.
Thank him for putting eternity in your heart.
Pray for the oppressed, and ask what he would have you do.
